title_full: Symphony No. 3 in E flat major, Op. 55 “Eroica”

composer.name: Ludwig van Beethoven
composer.nationality_note: Grove opens the article “German composer” (b Bonn, bap. 17 Dec 1770; d Vienna, 26 Mar 1827), and this set follows Grove. The label names the German cultural and linguistic nation, not a state: no German nation-state existed until 1871. Beethoven was born in Bonn, seat of the Electorate of Cologne — an Imperial state of the Holy Roman Empire, styled “of the German Nation” — and lived in Vienna from 1792 until his death. Across the composers in this set Grove's nationalities track the modern state that now holds the birthplace: Bonn and Hamburg give German (Beethoven, Brahms), Salzburg Austrian (Mozart), St Petersburg Russian (Shostakovich). Grove states no editorial rule for this, and does not always assign a nationality at all — Leopold Mozart, born in Augsburg, is simply “Composer, violinist and theorist”.

era_note: Kept Classical deliberately (decided 21 Aug 2026). periods.json buckets by year and the bucket sets the card colour; Romantic begins 1830, so all nine read Classical. The boundary is global, so moving it to split Beethoven would carry Haydn's late symphonies and the whole of Schubert across with him. Grove's three periods (first to c1802, second to c1812, third 1813-27) divide the nine 1-2 | 3-8 | 9, so the scholarly break falls at the Eroica, not at any date in the 1830s. This is where the line would fall if one were drawn. Grove calls the symphonic ideal the Eroica inaugurates ‘par excellence a Romantic phenomenon’, while allowing that the purely musical procedures may still be regarded as Classical. Romantic in ambition and Classical in method, from here on — which is why a single boundary cannot express it.

place.polity_note: Before 11 August 1804 there is no Austrian Empire: the sovereign entity is the composite Habsburg Monarchy, and the Archduchy of Austria sits within the Holy Roman Empire. The historical basemap labels these lands “Austrian Empire” in its 1783 and 1800 snapshots regardless, which is why the card takes its wording from here and not from the map data.
place.note: Grove gives 1803 and places him at Oberdöbling, a village outside Vienna, for the summer — 'not a happy summer for Beethoven, and for a time he may have thought of leaving Vienna altogether – perhaps for Paris.' Wikipedia's 1802–1804 span takes in sketches and final revisions.

reason.summary: Dedicated to Napoleon, then scratched out when he crowned himself Emperor.
reason.occasion: Conceived as a 'Bonaparte symphony'; the published dedication went to Lobkowitz, who had bought the exclusive rights.
reason.detail: Grove: the decision to embark on a 'Bonaparte symphony' at just this time 'came from inner pressures', not from the theatre contracts he was then negotiating. Wikipedia gives the familiar account of the withdrawn dedication in autumn 1804, after Napoleon declared himself Emperor, and the score's publication in 1806 as Sinfonia Eroica. Grove notes more is known about this work's composition than any other of Beethoven's, thanks to Nottebohm's monograph on the sketches.

first_performance.notes: First public performance. Grove records a private one earlier, at the Lobkowitz palace in the summer of 1804; Wikipedia dates that 9 June 1804. Grove does not give a day, so the record keeps the season.

listen_for.hook: A horn slips in with the theme four bars early — it sounds wrong.
listen_for.detail: The horn enters with the main theme over the dominant, against the strings' hushed tremolo, and was long taken for a copyist's error. Wikipedia: a horn 'famously appears to come in early with the main theme in E♭'.

listen_for.hook: It runs twice as long as any symphony before it.
listen_for.detail: Wikipedia: 'twice as long as the symphonies of Joseph Haydn and Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart', with the first movement alone about the length of a complete Classical symphony.

listen_for.hook: The second movement is a funeral march for a hero still living.
listen_for.detail: Wikipedia notes its range 'from the misery of the funeral march theme to the relative solace of happier, major-key episodes'.
